title: Through a glass (1 Corinthians 13:8–13)
hook: now we see through a glass darkly, then face to face

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's list of what charity does. Your line was charity is patient. Where did you wait one breath longer than usual? Day five hundred seventy-five.

Turn off a phone in a dark room and look at the black screen. You can see your face, sort of. A shape, shadows where the eyes are. That's close to what a mirror gave you in Corinth. Mirrors were polished metal, often bronze, and even a good one showed a dim, warm, slightly wobbly face. Paul has just said that charity never falls away. Now he explains why almost everything else will: because right now, even the wisest of us is looking at a reflection.
screen: `A FACE IN A BLACK SCREEN.` → `BRONZE MIRRORS IN CORINTH.` → `EVERYTHING ELSE WILL PASS.`

segments.voice: Prophecies will end, he says. Tongues will cease. Knowledge will be destroyed. We know in part and we prophesy in part, and when that which is perfect comes, the partial will be done away. Then he reaches for two pictures. The first is growing up: when I was a child, I spoke and thought like a child, and when I became a man I put away the things of a child. The second is the mirror: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I am known." The Greek behind in a dark manner is a phrase meaning in a riddle, and that word, ainigma, is where English gets enigma. So faith isn't blind. It sees something real, but indirectly, the way you solve a riddle. Look at the very end of the verse, too: even as I am known. Paul's hope isn't only that he'll finally understand God. It's that he is already fully known, and will one day know in the same way. The Church calls that final seeing the beatific vision. The Catechism says the saints in heaven see God face to face, as he is, and that this is the happiness of heaven. Then Paul closes the chapter: "And now there remain faith, hope, and charity, these three: but the greatest of these is charity." Why the greatest? Thomas Aquinas and many teachers after him give the same answer. Face to face, you no longer need faith in what you can't see, or hope for what you already have. Charity is the one that doesn't end.
screen: `WE KNOW IN PART.` · `A CHILD, THEN GROWN.` · `IN A RIDDLE: ENIGMA.` · `FACE TO FACE: THE BEATIFIC VISION.` · then, large: `THE GREATEST OF THESE IS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave one question unanswered. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you can't figure out right now. Why something happened. What comes next. What God is doing, if you believe in God. Don't try to solve it. Picture it as a face in an old bronze mirror: really there, but blurred. Let it stay blurred. Breathe with it. If you pray, you can hand it over with Paul's words, now I know in part. If you don't, simply let the not-knowing sit next to you without fighting it. The bell holds the time.
Through a glass. Paul's picture of how we know God now: a dim reflection in a metal mirror, until the day we see face to face. Today's word.
Your line: then, face to face. Today, when you hit something you can't explain, say I know in part, and let it rest there for now. Day five hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Catholics speak of the beatific vision, the sight of God face to face, as the final hope of the Christian life; the Church teaches the saints in heaven already enjoy it.

fork.setup: you're writing to Corinth: prophecy, tongues and knowledge will all pass. faith, hope and charity remain. which do you call the greatest?
options: knowledge, because it finally becomes complete.
fork.reveal: "the greatest of these is charity." face to face, faith and hope are fulfilled; charity goes on.

original.note: Greek: a riddle. 'in a dark manner' in 1 Corinthians 13:12 is literally 'in a riddle'; English gets 'enigma' from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old way of saying things look gloomy.
what it means: now we know God truly but dimly, like a face in a metal mirror; one day, face to face.
what a scholar hears: en ainigmati, in a riddle; the Church names the face-to-face seeing the beatific vision.
